title: OpenSanctions Pairs: A Large-Scale Dataset for Pairwise Entity Matching
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: Superficially near-identical records can refer to different entities, so name-based matching fails without unique identifiers.
layout: 2 side-by-side JSON panels, left-to-right, with a not-equal sign between
description: Two gray rectangular code-style panels sit side by side. Each shows a JSON record for a sanctioned individual from Pakistan's proscribed persons list, set in monospaced font. Both records have the same caption and name ("Khalid Mehmood"), the same dataset (pk_proscribed) and the same country (pk). They differ in the id and idNumber fields (3520114139885 on the left, 3710502620181 on the right), in fatherName (Muhammad Khan vs. Haji Muhammad), and in address (LAHORE vs. ATTOCK, Punjab). A large not-equal sign (≠) between the panels shows the two records are different people. The figure uses no color beyond gray and black. The eye goes first to the matching names, then to the ≠ sign, then to the differing fields. Ellipses mark truncated properties.
caption: Example entity pair illustrating the difficulty of pairwise matching. These two individuals on Pakistan's proscribed persons list share the exact same name, country, and sanctions program, yet they are different people with distinct national ID numbers and fathers. The Nomenklatura baseline assigned this pair a 0.98 match score, near the maximum possible, demonstrating how name-based matching fails for common names without unique identifiers.
abstract: We release OpenSanctions Pairs, the first large-scale public benchmark for entity matching on sanctions and OSINT data. The dataset includes 755,540 expert-labeled pairs over 1 million entities, aggregated from 293 source datasets across 45 jurisdictions. It captures real-world diversity in compliance data, spanning multiple languages and writing systems (e.g., Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic), inconsistent structure, and time-varying provenance, and is substantially more heterogeneous than prior entity matching benchmarks. As baselines, we evaluate the production rule-based matcher (nomenklatura RegressionV1) alongside open- and closed-weight LLMs on a single frozen analyst-judged split ($N=3{,}000$), with 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals and paired McNemar tests. The rule-based baseline reaches 85.8\% F1 and the strongest model (GPT-5.2 Pro) 98.1\%, but the top three frontier models are statistically indistinguishable, and a small open model suited to at-scale deployment (Llama-3.1-8B) trails the frontier by roughly 20 F1 points. The rule-based baseline and LLMs fail in complementary ways: rules over-match, while LLMs struggle with cross-script transliteration. Substantial headroom remains once the evaluation is made strict: an entity-disjoint split costs GPT-4o four F1 points (97.5 to 93.4), and cross-script pairs collapse weak models (Llama-3.1-8B falls to 59.4 F1) while frontier models hold near 96.5, so progress is needed on deployable-cost and cross-script matching rather than on the frontier alone.
